axes.name: Electronic state
axes.question: Which electronic state participates?
axes.note: Codes describe the electronic state involved in an event; S2 does not imply that the product remains a radical. S3 may overlap with S1 or S2.

axes.name: Orbital interaction
axes.question: What is the dominant electronic interaction?
axes.note: This is a teaching-level description, not a unique orbital decomposition. O2 and O4 can overlap; all reactions involve orbitals, while O3 specifically denotes pericyclic concerted interaction.

axes.name: Bond reorganization
axes.question: What changes in bonding are most prominent?
axes.note: This records the principal change, not a complete bond-change inventory. R1 can include local π-bond-order changes; consult the mechanism for detailed bond making and breaking.

axes.name: Nuclear geometry
axes.question: How do atoms approach and reorganize?
axes.note: A coarse grouping of prominent nuclear motion. G3 can also describe the planar-to-tetrahedral carbonyl change as a teaching model; such boundaries are candidates.

1111.label: Bond formation or cleavage
why: One principal bond formed or broken
1111.boundary: For SN1 ionization, O1 follows the project convention for polar electron-pair bookkeeping; it does not claim a new donor–acceptor bond forms during departure. Alkene protonation follows the same inherited convention; inspect the mechanism for the accompanying π-bond change.

1122.label: Polar bond replacement
why: Occupied orbital donates into an acceptor orbital
One bond is replaced by another
Approach and departure are coupled in one event
1122.boundary: SN2 and direct proton transfer can share this code; the code does not distinguish a carbon from a hydrogen reaction center.

2211.label: Radical bond formation
why: Approach at the reaction center dominates
2211.boundary: Radical addition can convert a π bond into a σ bond; radical recombination can ultimately yield a closed-shell product.

1333.label: Concerted pericyclic reorganization
1333.boundary: Concerted does not mean synchronous. This code cannot distinguish cycloaddition, electrocyclization, and σ migration, so retain the reaction name.

1113.label: Carbonyl addition / elimination
why: n or σ donation into π*; reverse process restores the carbonyl
Nucleophilic bond formation or leaving-group cleavage dominates
The carbonyl center changes between planar and tetrahedral geometry
1113.boundary: This is an early candidate assignment, not a fixed v0.1 code. R3 is another possible boundary when π-bond-order change is emphasized.

1133.label: Polar multiple-bond reorganization
why: Donor–acceptor interaction between base and substrate
C–H, C–X, and C=C bonding changes are coupled
Several centers adjust together or form a planar π system
1133.boundary: A project candidate used for E2 and the alkene-forming E1 event. Concerted E2 chemistry is not automatically a pericyclic O3 reaction.

2222.label: Radical atom transfer
why: Singly occupied orbital interacts with a σ bond
An atom transfers between reaction centers
2222.boundary: A project candidate for H- or halogen-atom transfer; this is not a quantum-chemically validated classification.

reactions.name: Proton transfer
reactions.conditions: Compare equilibrium in the same solvent and pKa scale.
reactions.summary: Proton transfer replaces an O–H bond with C–H bonding; it shares a broad 1122 code with SN2.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: The cyanide carbon lone pair abstracts the carboxylic-acid proton; the acid O–H bond pair returns to oxygen, yielding acetate and HCN.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: 10^(9.31 − 4.76) ≈ 3.55 × 10⁴ from the two approximate pKa values on a shared scale; not a measured equilibrium constant.
reactions.scope: pKa depends on solvent, temperature, and standard state; solution proton transfer can involve solvent relays.

reactions.name: SN2 substitution
reactions.conditions: Methyl substrate; nucleophilicity depends on solvent.
reactions.summary: C–O formation and C–Br cleavage occur together in one backside displacement.

steps.title: Backside displacement
steps.flow: The hydroxide oxygen lone pair attacks methyl carbon from behind; the C–Br bond pair departs with bromide in the same event.
steps.geometry: Nu–C–Br approaches a near-linear backside alignment.

facts: A chiral reaction center inverts configuration, but the R/S descriptor does not necessarily flip.
reactions.scope: Methyl carbon is achiral; hindrance can alter the competition between substitution and elimination.

literatureCases.title: SN2 electronic-structure comparison across C, N, O, and F centers
literatureCases.model: Cl⁻ + A–Cl, with A–Cl = CH₃Cl, NH₂Cl, OHCl, or FCl; gas phase.
literatureCases.relation: Related benchmark. This card uses HO⁻ + CH₃Br, so none of these numbers describes its substrate.
literatureCases.method: ZORA-OLYP/TZ2P; activation-strain analysis at the symmetric transition state for C, N, O and at the transition complex for F. The vacant σ*(A–Cl) energies refer to the isolated substrates under the authors’ orbital convention.
literatureCases.interpretation: The acceptor σ* orbital is lower in this series while the fragment interaction becomes more stabilizing. These are a specified orbital energy and an interaction-energy decomposition, not a transferable scalar “coupling degree.”
literatureCases.limits: Orbital energies depend on the method and orbital convention; the interaction term depends on the chosen fragments and geometry. The F entry is a transition complex rather than the same kind of stationary point as the first three. Values transcribed from Tables 3 and 4; no value for HO⁻ + CH₃Br is implied.

literatureInsights.method: CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVTZ energies on MP2/6-311++G(d,p) geometries; activation-strain and molecular-orbital analyses.
literatureInsights.finding: For this microsolvated ethyl chloride network, backside SN2 is preferred to anti-E2, and adding water increases the preference. E2 requires greater characteristic substrate distortion; solvation attenuates the fragment interaction.
literatureInsights.limits: The teaching card is HO⁻ + CH₃Br, so the computed preference and energies do not transfer.

reactions.name: SN1: ionization & capture
reactions.conditions: A substrate and medium that permit carbocation formation; illustrative formal anionic nucleophile.
reactions.summary: Ionization and nucleophilic capture are distinct events that happen to share the inherited 1111 code.

steps.title: Heterolytic ionization
steps.flow: The C–X bond pair goes to X, producing X⁻ and a carbocation.
steps.orbital: The σ(C–X) electron pair follows X during heterolysis; a vacant p-like orbital develops at carbon.
steps.geometry: C and leaving group separate; the carbocation center tends toward planar geometry.

steps.title: Carbocation capture
steps.flow: The nucleophile lone pair attacks the carbocation carbon and forms the new C–Nu σ bond.
steps.geometry: The nucleophile approaches one face of the approximately planar cation.

facts: 1111 → 1111; the same code does not mean the same event.
C–X heterolysis forms a p-like carbocation acceptor orbital.
reactions.scope: A formal core model, not a guarantee for every R₃C–X/Nu⁻ pair; strong bases may favor E2.
reactions.note: If Nu is water or an alcohol, oxonium deprotonation is normally required; see SN1 solvolysis.
reactions.mechanismNote: Follow the specified substrate and conditions through every listed event. Electron arrows and intermediates are described below; solvent-mediated proton transfer may group several microscopic transfers.

reactions.name: SN1 solvolysis
reactions.conditions: water / polar protic medium
reactions.summary: Ionization, water capture, and oxonium deprotonation produce neutral alcohol.

steps.title: Heterolytic ionization
steps.flow: The C–Br bond pair goes to bromine, producing Br⁻ and tert-butyl cation.
steps.orbital: The σ(C–X) electron pair follows X during heterolysis; a vacant p-like orbital develops at carbon.
steps.geometry: C and leaving group separate; the carbocation center tends toward planar geometry.

steps.title: Carbocation capture
steps.flow: Water donates an oxygen lone pair to the carbocation, giving a protonated alcohol (oxonium).
steps.geometry: The nucleophile approaches one face of the approximately planar cation.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: A second water molecule removes a proton from oxonium; its O–H bond pair returns to the alcohol oxygen, yielding tert-butanol and H₃O⁺.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: Lone-pair donation enters the vacant p-like orbital; ion pairing can alter the electronic structure.
reactions.scope: E1 can compete. Chiral SN1 substrates often partially racemize; ion pairs may bias attack from each face.

reactions.name: E2 elimination
reactions.conditions: Strong base and access to an anti-periplanar conformation.
reactions.summary: Three electron-pair movements couple in a single anti-favored elimination event.

steps.title: Concerted β-elimination
steps.flow: Ethoxide abstracts a β-H; the C–H pair forms C=C while the C–Br pair goes to Br⁻, all in one concerted event.
steps.orbital: n(base) → σ*(C–H), coupled with σ(C–H) → σ*(C–Br).
steps.geometry: An anti-periplanar H–C–C–Br alignment is generally favored.

facts: Base lone-pair donation into σ*(C–H) is coupled with σ(C–H) donation into σ*(C–Br).
The anti-periplanar arrangement aligns the breaking and forming interactions.
reactions.scope: 1133 is a candidate code. Anti geometry is usually favored, though syn elimination can occur in suitable systems.

reactions.name: Lithium aluminum hydride reduction
reactions.conditions: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, followed by H₂O work-up.

steps.title: Carbonyl coordination to aluminum

steps.title: Intracomplex hydride transfer
steps.flow: The Al–H bond pair transfers hydride character to carbonyl carbon; the C=O π pair shifts to O and an aluminum alkoxide forms.
steps.geometry: Planar carbonyl carbon becomes tetrahedral as C–H and O–Al contacts form.

steps.title: Aqueous work-up releases the alcohol
steps.flow: Water protonates the alkoxide oxygen; hydrolysis breaks the Al–O contact and releases the alcohol.
steps.geometry: Protonation and Al–O hydrolysis complete aqueous work-up.

facts: LiAlH₄; the displayed donor is AlH₄⁻.
Anhydrous ether during reduction; water is introduced only in the work-up.
The aluminate is a stoichiometric intermediate, not free H⁻ in solution.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation
reactions.conditions: Textbook CN⁻-catalyzed pathway with HCN as proton donor.
reactions.summary: Cyanide attack gives an alkoxide; protonation from HCN regenerates CN⁻.

steps.title: Nucleophilic carbonyl addition
steps.flow: The carbon end of CN⁻ attacks carbonyl carbon; the C=O π pair shifts to oxygen, producing the cyano alkoxide.
steps.geometry: The carbonyl center changes from approximately trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Alkoxide oxygen removes H from HCN; the H–C bond pair returns to carbon to regenerate CN⁻ and form cyanohydrin.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: CN⁻ is consumed in addition and regenerated on protonation.
reactions.scope: The carbon of CN⁻ attacks. The 1113 addition code is a candidate; a prochiral carbonyl gives a racemate in an achiral medium.

reactions.summary: Acyl substitution proceeds through addition and collapse of a tetrahedral intermediate.

steps.title: Nucleophilic carbonyl addition
steps.flow: Alkoxide attacks the acyl carbon; the C=O π pair shifts to oxygen, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.

reactions.name: Aldol addition
reactions.conditions: Base-catalyzed addition ending at the β-hydroxy aldehyde.
reactions.summary: Enolate formation, carbonyl attack, and protonation yield a β-hydroxy aldehyde.

steps.flow: Base removes an α-H; the C–H electrons enter the delocalized enolate system rather than making a separate intermediate for each resonance form.

literatureCases.title: Orbital interaction and electron donation in a Diels–Alder model
literatureCases.model: 1,3-Butadiene + acrolein (neutral O) versus 1,3-butadiene + acrolein radical cation (O•⁺).
literatureCases.relation: Related dienophile. The teaching reaction on this card uses ethene, and the radical-cation pathway is a distinct open-shell mechanism.
literatureCases.method: ZORA-(U)BP86/TZ2P; fragments are butadiene and acrolein/acrolein radical cation. EDA evaluated at matched transition-state-like geometries with forming C(diene)···Cβ(dienophile) = 2.203 Å.
literatureCases.interpretation: At the matched geometry, ionization changes the EDA orbital term by −27.5 kcal/mol and reduces Pauli repulsion by 18.8 kcal/mol. In the open-shell case, the butadiene π-HOMO and acrolein-cation SOMO have reported overlap S = 0.05 and about 0.7 electron donated into the SOMO under this analysis. The neutral path is concerted asynchronous; the radical-cation path becomes stepwise.
literatureCases.limits: ΔEorbital is the total EDA orbital-interaction term, S is a dimensionless overlap, and 0.7 electron is a method-specific charge-transfer analysis. None is a diabatic electronic-coupling matrix element H_DA or an intrinsic SORG score. The radical-cation pathway is not assigned the neutral card’s 1333 code.

reactions.conditions: thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement
reactions.summary: A six-center [3,3] shift changes one σ bond and two π bonds together.

steps.flow: Across a six-center array, the O–allyl σ bond breaks, two π bonds shift, and a new C–C σ bond forms in one [3,3] rearrangement.

reactions.name: Bromination of an alkene
reactions.conditions: Br₂ in an inert solvent; no water or alcohol as competing nucleophile.
reactions.summary: Bromonium formation followed by backside bromide opening gives anti dibromide.

steps.title: Bromonium-ion formation
steps.flow: The alkene π pair attacks one Br of Br₂, the Br–Br pair goes to the other Br, and a lone pair on the attached Br bridges the second alkene carbon to form bromonium.
steps.geometry: One bromine bridges both carbons in a three-membered ion; no free carbocation is required.

steps.title: Backside bromide ring opening
steps.flow: Br⁻ attacks a bromonium carbon from behind; that C–Br bridge pair returns to the bridging bromine, opening the ring with anti addition.
steps.geometry: Backside opening places the two bromines anti and removes the bridge.

facts: Cyclic bromonium ion, not a free carbocation.
Anti addition; a cyclic alkene gives trans vicinal dibromide.

reactions.name: Halohydrin formation
reactions.conditions: Br₂ in water; water is the competing nucleophile and solvent.

reactions.name: Nitration of benzene
reactions.conditions: concentrated HNO₃ / H₂SO₄; electrophile is NO₂⁺.
reactions.summary: Nitronium generation, aromatic attack, and deprotonation restore the aromatic ring.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: A nitric-acid oxygen lone pair takes H from sulfuric acid; the acid O–H pair returns to sulfate.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Nitronium-ion formation
steps.flow: Protonated nitric acid loses water: the N–OH₂ bond breaks and the remaining oxygens form linear NO₂⁺.
steps.orbital: σ(N–OH₂⁺) cleavage; nitronium π system forms
steps.geometry: Dehydration produces the near-linear NO₂⁺ electrophile.

steps.title: Aromatic attack and σ-complex formation
steps.flow: A benzene π pair attacks nitronium nitrogen to form C–N and an arenium (σ) complex; its resonance contributors are one intermediate.
steps.geometry: The attacked carbon becomes approximately tetrahedral and the σ complex loses aromaticity.

steps.title: Deprotonation restores aromaticity
steps.flow: HSO₄⁻ removes H from the substituted ring carbon; the C–H pair restores aromatic π bonding and regenerates H₂SO₄.
steps.geometry: The conjugated aromatic ring becomes planar again.

facts: Nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, generated by the acid mixture.
Lost in the σ-complex step and restored by deprotonation.
reactions.scope: A textbook benzene model; substituents change orientation, and electrophile-generation equilibria depend on water content.

reactions.name: Fischer esterification
reactions.conditions: acid-catalyzed; water removal or alcohol excess can shift the equilibrium.
reactions.summary: Acid activation, alcohol addition, proton transfers, water loss, and catalyst regeneration form ester.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: The carbonyl oxygen takes H from acid; the acid X–H bond pair returns to its conjugate base.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Nucleophilic carbonyl addition
steps.flow: Ethanol oxygen attacks the activated acyl carbon; the C=O π pair shifts to the original carbonyl oxygen, giving tetrahedral oxonium.
steps.geometry: The carbonyl center changes from approximately trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Solvent-mediated proton transfers neutralize the ethoxy oxygen and turn one OH group into an H₂O leaving group.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate
steps.flow: The other oxygen lone pair reforms C=O while the C–OH₂ pair leaves with water, producing protonated ester.
steps.geometry: The tetrahedral acyl center reforms a planar carbonyl in protonated ester.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Water removes the remaining carbonyl-oxygen proton; its O–H pair returns to ester oxygen and acid is regenerated.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: Acid-catalyzed nucleophilic acyl substitution with a tetrahedral intermediate.
The reaction is reversible; water removal or excess alcohol favors ester.
reactions.scope: Solvent-mediated proton relays are grouped as one teaching event; microscopic relays can involve multiple alcohol/water molecules.

reactions.name: Imine formation from a ketone
reactions.conditions: mild acid catalysis; avoid strongly acidic conditions that fully protonate the amine.
reactions.summary: Amine addition to activated carbonyl, proton transfers, dehydration, and deprotonation form imine.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Acid protonates carbonyl oxygen, increasing electrophilicity; too much acid would suppress amine nucleophilicity.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Nucleophilic carbonyl addition
steps.flow: Methylamine nitrogen attacks carbonyl carbon; the C=O π pair goes to oxygen, giving carbinolammonium.
steps.geometry: The carbonyl center changes from approximately trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Water removes a proton from nitrogen to form neutral carbinolamine.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Acid protonates the hydroxyl oxygen so it can leave as water.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Dehydration to the iminium ion
steps.flow: The nitrogen lone pair makes C=N as the C–OH₂ bond pair leaves with water, forming an iminium ion.
steps.geometry: C=N forms while water departs, leaving an iminium center.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Water removes the final N–H proton; the N–H pair returns to nitrogen to form neutral imine and regenerate acid.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: Mild acid activates the carbonyl while leaving enough free amine nucleophile.
reactions.scope: Reversible; removing water drives imine formation. Proton transfers can involve solvent relays.

reactions.name: Base-catalyzed aldol condensation
reactions.conditions: acetone under basic conditions; dehydration gives mesityl oxide.
reactions.summary: Aldol addition followed by E1cB dehydration gives a conjugated enone.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Base removes an acetone α-H, sending the C–H pair into the delocalized enolate system.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Nucleophilic carbonyl addition
steps.flow: Enolate α-carbon bonds to a second acetone carbonyl carbon; its C=O π pair moves to oxygen.
steps.geometry: The carbonyl center changes from approximately trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Alkoxide takes H from water, forming diacetone alcohol and regenerating hydroxide.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Base removes another α-H to make the enolate precursor of dehydration.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: E1cB loss of hydroxide
steps.flow: Enolate α-carbon electrons form Cα=Cβ as the β-C–O bond pair leaves with HO⁻, giving conjugated mesityl oxide.
steps.geometry: A C=C bond conjugated with carbonyl forms; base is regenerated over the cycle.

facts: Enolate → β-hydroxy ketone (diacetone alcohol) → enone (mesityl oxide).
Dehydration is a distinct E1cB sequence after aldol addition.
reactions.scope: Substrate, temperature, and base decide whether addition product persists or dehydration follows.

reactions.name: Acid-catalyzed epoxide opening
reactions.conditions: aqueous acid; chloride is the nucleophile.
reactions.summary: Epoxide protonation, backside chloride opening, and deprotonation give chlorohydrin.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.equation: propylene oxide + H₃O⁺ ⇌ protonated propylene oxide + H₂O
steps.flow: Epoxide oxygen takes a proton from acid, activating ring C–O bonds for opening.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

steps.title: Chloride opens the protonated epoxide
steps.flow: Cl⁻ attacks the more substituted carbon from behind; that ring C–O pair goes to oxygen and the ring opens with inversion at the attacked carbon.
steps.geometry: The attacked carbon inverts as C–Cl forms and the ring opens from behind.

steps.title: Proton transfer
steps.flow: Water removes the oxonium proton; its O–H pair returns to product oxygen to give neutral chlorohydrin and regenerate acid.
steps.geometry: The base approaches H as the original donor–H contact weakens.

facts: Acidic opening commonly favors attack at the more substituted carbon; substrate effects matter.
Backside ring opening gives inversion at the attacked carbon and anti relationship.
reactions.scope: Propylene oxide and HCl illustrate an acid-promoted path with regioselectivity and backside stereochemistry; a free carbocation is not required.
